definition.text: The usefulness of a thing: the features that let it satisfy a human want or need, a concept from classical and Marxist economics.

facts.text: Gold, for example, can serve as money, as decoration or as an excellent electrical conductor.
Adam Smith noted that diamonds have high exchange value but little use, while water is very useful yet cheap.
For Marx, every commodity is both a use value and an exchange value, the proportion in which it trades for other goods.
Turning a use value into a commodity needs preconditions: it must be tradable, ownership must be securely transferable, and there must be real demand.
Marginalist economics later treated use value as coming from the marginal utility consumers find in a good.
Critics of the commodification of nature draw on the Marxian idea that commodities embody both use and exchange value.

title: Anthropocentrism

definition.text: The belief that human beings are the central or most important beings on the planet.

facts.text: From this view humans are separate from and superior to nature, and animals, plants and minerals are resources for human use.
Environmental ethics often treats it as the root cause of human-made problems in the ecosphere.
Its defenders argue that a sound long-term view keeps the environment suitable for humans, and that the real problem is shallow anthropocentrism.
William Grey called for an enriched human-centred idea of human interest to replace short-term, self-regarding views.
Val Plumwood compared its role in green theory to that of androcentrism in feminist theory.
The word 'dominion' in Genesis has been used to justify it, though some now see it as a possible mistranslation.
Pope Francis's 2023 Laudate Deum speaks of a preferable 'situated anthropocentrism'.
J. Howard Moore argued in 1906 that Darwin's theory of common descent 'sealed the doom' of anthropocentrism.

contested_note: Environmental philosophers dispute whether human-centred thinking causes ecological harm or whether only its shallow, short-term form does.
